books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: James K. Polk, Inaugural Address, March 4, 1845

stimulus.source_note: James K. Polk, Inaugural Address, March 4, 1845. Public domain.
stimulus.text: Texas was once a part of our country — was unwisely ceded away to a foreign power — is now independent, and possesses an undoubted right to dispose of a part or the whole of her territory and to merge her sovereignty as a separate and independent state in ours... To enlarge its limits is to extend the dominions of peace over additional territories and increasing millions... Nor will it become in a less degree my duty to assert and maintain by all constitutional means the right of the United States to that portion of our territory which lies beyond the Rocky Mountains. Our title to the country of the Oregon is “clear and unquestionable,” and already are our people preparing to perfect that title by occupying it with their wives and children.

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim excerpt from James K. Polk, Inaugural Address, March 4, 1845, public domain
stem: The passage as a whole most directly shows that Polk viewed expansion as

options.text: a dangerous gamble that might lead the country into war.
options.misconception: Polk presents expansion as peaceful and rightful, not as a dangerous gamble.

options.text: a question to be settled by the states, not the federal government.
options.misconception: Polk speaks as president claiming national title; he does not hand the question to the states.

options.text: the peaceful spread of American government over more land and people.
a policy that should wait until the slavery question was settled.
options.misconception: Polk presses for annexation and Oregon at once; he does not say to wait for the slavery debate.

rationales.A: Polk calls enlargement an extension of “the dominions of peace,” so he presents it as peaceful, not as a gamble.
rationales.B: Polk claims the title himself as president; the speech is a national claim, not a matter left to the states.
rationales.C: Polk says enlarging the country extends “the dominions of peace over additional territories and increasing millions” — government spreading peacefully over land and people.
rationales.D: Polk urges annexation and the Oregon claim immediately, in his first address as president, with no waiting for the slavery question.
rationales.general:
1. Listen to Polk's language. Enlarging the country extends “the dominions of peace” over new territories and millions of people.
2. Notice the tone. Nothing here warns of danger or delay; the tone is confident and welcoming.
3. Match the tone to the choices. Only one choice describes expansion as peaceful growth.
Remember: a president's first speech tells you how he wants the country to see his policy — here, as peace spreading, not war coming.
